PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

**Sacramento, Calif.** – Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., assigned proposition numbers today to the legislative and initiative measures set to appear on the November 3, 2026, General Election ballot.

## California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., Announces the Statewide Voter Information Guide for the November 3, 2026, General Election Is Available for Public Review
**Sacramento, Calif.** – Today California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., made the November 3, 2026, California General Election Official Voter Information Guide available for public review.
The guide, which will be mailed to every voting household in California, includes information about propositions and statements from candidates running for constitutional offices, as well as other important election information such as the California Voter Bill of Rights and information about how eligible Californians can vote.
California’s Official Voter Information Guide is available in 10 languages—English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.
The guide is available for public examination from July 21, 2026 through August 10, 2026 at https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display and at the Office of the Secretary of State’s Sacramento and Los Angeles locations.
During this public display period, any elector can challenge any portion of the Official Voter Information Guide in Sacramento Superior Court.
Following the conclusion of the public examination period, the Office of the Secretary of State will begin printing and mailing the statewide Voter Information Guide to all households that have at least one registered voter.

Proposition 45 will:
- Require disclosure by making public the documents filed by insurers to justify rate increases.
- Promote transparency by allowing public hearings and the right to challenge unjustified premium increases.

Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

## Healthcare Insurance. Rate Changes. Initiative Statute.
- Requires changes to health insurance rates, or anything else affecting the charges associated with health insurance, to be approved by Insurance Commissioner before taking effect.
- Provides for public notice, disclosure, and hearing on health insurance rate changes, and subsequent judicial review.
- Requires sworn statement by health insurer as to accuracy of information submitted to Insurance Commissioner to justify rate changes.
- Does not apply to employer large group health plans.
- Prohibits health, auto, and homeowners insurers from determining policy eligibility or rates based on lack of prior coverage or credit history.

INITIATIVE STATUTE.** Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review of specified project categories (including most housing, transportation, water, health, and clean energy projects).
For these types of projects, this measure:
- sets deadlines for public agencies to complete environmental review and take required actions for project;
- allows expedited review of project’s environmental impacts, limiting public agencies’ current obligation to consider a range of feasible project alternatives to reduce environmental impacts; and

## California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., Announces the Statewide Voter Information Guide for the November 3, 2026, General Election Is Available for Public Review
**Sacramento, Calif.** – Today California Secretary of State Shirley N. Weber, Ph.D., made the November 3, 2026, California General Election Official Voter Information Guide available for public review.
The guide, which will be mailed to every voting household in California, includes information about propositions and statements from candidates running for constitutional offices, as well as other important election information such as the California Voter Bill of Rights and information about how eligible Californians can vote.
California’s Official Voter Information Guide is available in 10 languages—English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Khmer, Korean, Tagalog, Thai, and Vietnamese.
The guide is available for public examination from July 21, 2026 through August 10, 2026 at https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/public-display and at the Office of the Secretary of State’s Sacramento and Los Angeles locations.
During this public display period, any elector can challenge any portion of the Official Voter Information Guide in Sacramento Superior Court.
Following the conclusion of the public examination period, the Office of the Secretary of State will begin printing and mailing the statewide Voter Information Guide to all households that have at least one registered voter.

Proposition 45 requires health insurance companies to open their books and publicly justify rate hikes, under penalty of perjury, *before* they can raise premiums for 5.8 million individual consumers and small business owners.
Proposition 45 will:
- Require disclosure by making public the documents filed by insurers to justify rate increases.
- Promote transparency by allowing public hearings and the right to challenge unjustified premium increases.
- Create accountability by giving the insurance commissioner authority to reject excessive rate increases and order refunds.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

**California Proposition 45 (November 3, 2026)** — "Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects" (CEQA reform), sponsored by CalChamber.

Evidence:
1. **PPIC October 16–22, 2026 poll** (1,086 likely voters, ±3.8%): 46% yes, 50% no, 4% undecided. This is the most recent high-quality nonpartisan poll, and shows the measure trailing for the first time.
2. **Trend**: 73% yes (July, generic language) → 49% yes/46% no (September, ballot language) → 46% yes/50% no (late October). Clear downward trend.
3. **A second poll (Probolsky?)** mentioned by South Bay Chronicle's "final weekend: two polls, two different answers" — let me note one had it ahead. The headline says "two polls, two different answers" — PPIC behind, Probolsky ahead perhaps. Hmm. But the aggregate:
4. **OnPoint Politics forecast (Nov 2, 2026)**: Yes chance to pass 47.8%, No 52.3%. Polling average 48.3% yes. Slight edge to No.
5. **Manifold prediction market**: 30% chance of passing.
6. **California initiative dynamics**: undecided voters historically break toward No; measures below 50% in late polling rarely pass. A measure polling at 46% with undecideds at 4% — undecideds typically split heavily No on complex initiatives, especially with "guts environmental law" messaging. The No side needs 50%+ of votes cast; even a small undecided break keeps No ahead.
7. Money favors Yes ($40M vs $20M), but the trend and late polling favor No.

One caveat: the South Bay Chronicle mentions a Probolsky poll showing a different answer (maybe yes ahead). Let me quickly check that article to be thorough. But even with a mixed final poll, the preponderance of evidence (PPIC 46/50, forecast 47.8% yes, Manifold 30%, undecided-break-no conventional wisdom) points to No being more likely to win.

Let me quickly fetch the South Bay Chronicle article to see the Probolsky numbers, for thoroughness.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.

A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.

A measure polling at 46% with undecideds at 4% — undecideds typically split heavily No on complex initiatives, especially with "guts environmental law" messaging. The No side needs 50%+ of votes cast; even a small undecided break keeps No ahead.
7. Money favors Yes ($40M vs $20M), but the trend and late polling favor No.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

PROP
45
MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars—potentially exceeding $100 million—annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters: California Children’s Hospital Association; California Water Association; California Council for Affordable Housing Opponents: Coalition for Clean Air; CA Environmental Voters; Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA; National Wildlife Federation
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Certain public and private projects would be eligible for new project review and court challenge procedures. For example, new procedures would tighten time limits for environmental review and reduce the scope of what courts can consider when reviewing legal challenges.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Public and private projects would continue to use existing project review and court challenge procedures.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
The failing status quo is making California unaffordable. Prop. 45 fixes our broken system and lowers our high cost of living by cutting red tape to build housing, water, schools, hospitals, clean energy, and wildfire prevention faster—while maintaining California’s strong environmental protections. Vote YES for a more affordable California. YESonProp45.com
CON
PROPOSITION 45 LIMITS ENVIRONMENTAL AND PUBLIC REVIEW OF PROJECTS BUILT IN YOUR COMMUNITY. It guts The California Environmental Quality Act—flipping California law to protect corporate profits over public health and our air and water. Prop. 45 won’t lower your costs: its utility and corporate funders profit while taxpayers pay more. VOTE NO.

Prop 45’s final weekend: two polls, two different answers, and a Bay Area that is the measure’s toughest crowd
PPIC’s October survey has the CEQA overhaul trailing 46% to 50% among likely voters, down from a narrow lead in September. A Probolsky Research poll has it narrowly ahead. Probolsky finds the Bay Area the most skeptical region.
November 1, 2026
Top image: The California State Capitol in Sacramento. Photo: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:California_State_Capitol_from_Capitol_Mall_-_Sacramento_(26429122855).jpg)
By Gideon Paley (https://southbaychronicle.com/reporters/#gideon-paley), Real Estate Development Reporter
ANALYSIS | What the late polling shows on the CEQA overhaul
Prop 45 heads into the last weekend before Tuesday’s election as a close race in the polls. The measure would put deadlines on environmental review and lawsuits under the California Environmental Quality Act for housing, water, energy and other projects it defines as essential.
PPIC: behind, and slipping
The Public Policy Institute of California’s October statewide survey, taken Oct. 16-22, found 46% of likely voters would vote yes, 50% no and 4% undecided, according to PPIC (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/). In September the same survey had the measure ahead, 49% to 46%. The October likely-voter sample was 1,086, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points, so the race is within that range.
The partisan split runs the opposite way from many California housing fights. A majority of Republicans support the measure, while 54% of Democrats oppose it, PPIC found. Gov. Gavin Newsom has stayed on the sidelines, The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) reported. PPIC also measured Prop 40 at 46% yes and 52% no.
Housing under construction at San Francisco’s former Upper Yard site in May 2022. Photo: Pi.1415926535 / CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upper_Yard_housing_construction,_May_2022.jpg)
Probolsky: ahead, barely
A Probolsky Research poll released Oct. 27 points the other way. The firm headlined its findings “Yes on Prop. 45 leads by a thin margin (https://www.probolskyresearch.com/2026/10/27/yes-on-prop-45-leads-by-a-thin-margin/).” It has not published full toplines, and it says it has no client in the race. Men back the measure 51% to 36%, while women oppose it 42% to 36%, the firm reported.
Probolsky also found the Bay Area to be the measure’s weakest region. “The Bay Area has some of the highest housing costs, yet that’s the region where the highest opposition shows up,” Probolsky said in its release.
The money
Both sides are spending heavily. Filings with the Fair Political Practices Commission as of Oct. 29 showed about $39.6 million raised for the Yes side and about $36.3 million for the No side. The Chronicle’s analysis of who is funding each side (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/31/analysis-who-is-funding-prop-45-and-why/) breaks down the largest donors.
Transmission lines carry power from the Encina Power Plant in Carlsbad. Prop. 45 would also cover energy and water projects, not only housing. Photo: Chris Hunkeler from Carlsbad, California, USA / CC BY-SA 2.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0) via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Transmission_Lines_(8550788014).jpg)
What supporters and opponents argue
Supporters say CEQA lawsuits and open-ended reviews have become a main cause of delay and cost for new housing and infrastructure, and that firm deadlines would get projects built faster. Opponents, including environmental and some labor groups, say the measure would weaken a key tool communities use to challenge harmful projects. The Chronicle’s editorial board has recommended a No vote (https://southbaychronicle.com/2026/10/25/editorial-vote-no-on-prop-45/). That editorial is separate from this newsroom’s reporting.
What to watch Tuesday
The two polls together suggest the result could come down to turnout, especially among Democrats who are splitting from their usual allies and among Bay Area voters. Many California mail ballots are counted after Election Day, so a close statewide measure may not be called on election night.

content.text:
**Research summary — California Proposition 45 (Nov 3, 2026): "Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects" (CEQA reform initiative)**

Evidence gathered:
- **PPIC poll (Oct 16–22, the gold-standard nonpartisan survey, 1,086 likely voters):** 46% yes / 50% no / 4% undecided — the first time the measure has trailed, down from 49–46 ahead in September and 73% in July (with generic language). Clear downward trend.
- **Probolsky Research poll (Oct 27):** Yes narrowly ahead, but full toplines not published.
- **OnPoint Politics forecast (Nov 2):** No slightly favored — Yes has a 47.8% chance to pass, No 52.3%.
- **Manifold prediction market:** ~30% chance of passing.
- **Structural factors:** Spending is roughly even (~$40M each side); the Democratic Party and environmental groups oppose it; Gov. Newsom stayed neutral. Critically, California initiatives polling below 50% in late October rarely pass — undecided voters historically break heavily toward "no" (status quo bias), and the yes side sits at only 46% in the best poll with a deteriorating trend.

The preponderance of evidence favors the "No" side.
